claims.text: The starting material is a crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticle containing five or more metals.
The intervention is the introduction of an HEA coating on the nanoparticle surface.
An HEA coating will enhance nanoparticle stability during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
The HEA coating reduces nanoparticle surface energy.
The HEA coating increases cohesion between nanoparticles.
Reduced surface energy and increased interparticle cohesion prevent nanoparticle agglomeration.
Reduced surface energy and increased interparticle cohesion prevent nanoparticle sintering.
The HEA cocktail effect can improve catalytic activity.
The HEA cocktail effect can improve catalytic selectivity.
Strengthened CO adsorption is responsible for improved catalytic performance.
Sluggish diffusion contributes to improved catalytic performance.
Lattice distortion contributes to improved catalytic performance.
HEA-coated nanoparticles will be more stable than untreated nanoparticles.
HEA-coated nanoparticles will have better catalytic performance than untreated nanoparticles.
The proposed characterization protocol includes in situ XAFS and XRD under hydrogen at 200–400 °C, H2-TPR to 600 °C, CO-TPD, FTIR, electron microscopy, and ETEM.
Failure to enhance both stability and catalytic performance would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The claimed operating regime is 773–1173 K (500–900 °C), but the principal in situ XAFS/XRD experiment is specified at only 200–400 °C, below that regime. H2-TPR reaches 600 °C only during a temperature ramp and does not test sustained operation across the claimed range.

Increasing cohesion between separate nanoparticles would ordinarily favor interparticle attachment rather than explain prevention of agglomeration; the proposed causal direction is internally incoherent without distinguishing coating-to-core cohesion from particle-to-particle cohesion.
